candidate.answerReason: The two inradii are 3/(3+√2) and 4/(4+√2). Their ratio simplifies to 3(10-√2)/28.

methods.label: Method 1: Use areas and semiperimeters
methods.explanation:
An incircle radius can be found from a triangle's area and perimeter. Joining the incenter to the three vertices divides the triangle into three triangles, each with height equal to the inradius \(r\). Thus
\[
K=\frac12r(\text{perimeter})=rs,
\]
where \(K\) is the area and \(s\) is the semiperimeter.

First find the dimensions of the two smaller triangles. Drop perpendiculars from \(D\) to \(AC\) and \(BC\). Their lengths are equal because \(D\) lies on the angle bisector; call this common length \(t>0\). Since \(AC\perp BC\), the perpendiculars form a square with \(C\) and \(D\) as opposite vertices. Therefore \(CD=t\sqrt2\).

The area of \(ABC\) is \(3\cdot4/2=6\). Adding the areas of the two smaller triangles gives
\[
6=\frac12(3)t+\frac12(4)t,
\]
so \(t=12/7\). Hence
\[
CD=\frac{12\sqrt2}{7},\qquad K_a=\frac{18}{7},\qquad K_b=\frac{24}{7}.
\]
The two triangles have the same altitude to \(AB\), so \(AD:DB=K_a:K_b=3:4\). Since \(AB=5\), this gives \(AD=15/7\) and \(DB=20/7\).

Their semiperimeters are consequently
\[
s_a=\frac{3+15/7+12\sqrt2/7}{2}=\frac{6(3+\sqrt2)}7,
\]
\[
s_b=\frac{4+20/7+12\sqrt2/7}{2}=\frac{6(4+\sqrt2)}7.
\]
Using \(r=K/s\), we obtain
\[
r_a=\frac3{3+\sqrt2},\qquad r_b=\frac4{4+\sqrt2}.
\]
All these quantities are positive. Rationalizing the resulting ratio gives
\[
\frac{r_a}{r_b}=\frac{3(4+\sqrt2)}{4(3+\sqrt2)}
=\frac{3(4+\sqrt2)(3-\sqrt2)}{4(9-2)}
=\boxed{\frac3{28}(10-\sqrt2)},
\]
choice E.
methods.levelReason: Derives the inradius-area relation from elementary triangle areas and uses only angle-bisector distances, square geometry, and the Pythagorean theorem.

methods.label: Method 2: Compare tangent lengths from C
methods.explanation:
The two smaller triangles have equal angles at \(C\). This lets us compare their inradii through similar right triangles formed by their incircles.

First, the angle-bisector theorem gives \(AD:DB=AC:BC=3:4\). Since \(AB=5\),
\[
AD=\frac{15}{7},\qquad DB=\frac{20}{7}.
\]
To find \(CD\), let \(t\) be the common perpendicular distance from \(D\) to \(AC\) and \(BC\). These distances are equal by the angle-bisector property. The areas of \(ADC\) and \(BCD\) add to \(6\), so
\[
\frac12(3)t+\frac12(4)t=6,
\]
and \(t=12/7\). The perpendiculars form a square with diagonal \(CD\), giving \(CD=12\sqrt2/7\).

Let \(I_a,I_b\) be the two incenters, and let their incircles touch \(CD\) at \(X_a,X_b\), respectively. Both \(CI_a\) and \(CI_b\) bisect a \(45^\circ\) angle. Also, the radii to \(X_a\) and \(X_b\) are perpendicular to \(CD\). Thus right triangles \(CX_aI_a\) and \(CX_bI_b\) are similar, and
\[
\frac{r_a}{r_b}=\frac{CX_a}{CX_b}.
\]
Tangent segments from the same vertex have equal lengths. In any triangle, adding the two sides from \(C\) and subtracting the opposite side therefore leaves twice the tangent length from \(C\). Applying this to the two triangles gives
\[
CX_a=\frac{AC+CD-AD}{2}=\frac{3+6\sqrt2}{7},
\]
\[
CX_b=\frac{BC+CD-DB}{2}=\frac{4+6\sqrt2}{7}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\frac{r_a}{r_b}=\frac{3+6\sqrt2}{4+6\sqrt2}
=\frac{(3+6\sqrt2)(6\sqrt2-4)}{72-16}
=\boxed{\frac3{28}(10-\sqrt2)},
\]
choice E.
methods.levelReason: Uses elementary tangent lengths and similar right triangles to compare radii, with no trigonometry.
